The *Gopālaka Sutta* (Ud 4.3; PTS Ud 38) is the third discourse in the fourth chapter (Meghiya Vagga) of the *Udāna* [SuttaCentral]. The narrative describes a cowherd who, after making a food offering to the Buddha and the monastic community, is abruptly murdered [SuttaCentral]. In response to this event, the Buddha utters an inspired verse of teaching (*udāna*) on the nature of the mind and harm [SuttaCentral]. The provided secondary literature references do not discuss this discourse, referring instead to the homonymous *Mahāgopālaka Sutta* (MN 33) and *Cūḷagopālaka Sutta* (MN 34) of the Majjhima Nikāya.
According to SuttaCentral, the verse found in the *Gopālaka Sutta* has a direct canonical parallel in Dhammapada verse 42 (Dhp 42), as well as resembling parallels in the *Cittavarga* ("Mind Chapter") of the Sanskrit and Tibetan *Udānavarga* traditions (UV 31, UVS 31, and Uv Kg 31) [SuttaCentral]. In addition, DharmaNexus identifies substantial internal text reuse across 62 Pali canonical texts, consisting largely of standardized narrative stock phrases describing meal offerings and departures [DharmaNexus]. The longest matching passages occur in the *Bhesajjakkhandhaka* of the Khandhaka (Kd 6 §3.1–5.2), the *Mahāparinibbāna Sutta* (DN 16 §2.1–5.1), the *Senāsanakkhandhaka* (Kd 16), the *Cunda Sutta* (Ud 8.5), and several other discourses in the Dīgha, Majjhima, and Aṅguttara Nikāyas [DharmaNexus]. DharmaNexus also aligns segments of this text with parallels in the Sanskrit *Saṅghabhedavastu* and *Divyāvadāna*, the Tibetan translation of the *Pratimokṣasūtraṭīkāvinayasamuccaya* (D4106), and Chinese Āgama collections such as the *Madhyama-āgama* (T 26) and *Saṃyukta-āgama* (T 99) [DharmaNexus].
